about.heading: About Cascadas de Tocoihue
about.lead: Welcome to the Cascadas de Tocoihue, widely recognized as the central Tocoihue. Located in the heart of Dalcahue, Los Lagos Region, Chile, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the Isla Grande de Chiloé.

location.heading: Location & How to Visit Tocoihue in Dalcahue
location.text: The Cascadas de Tocoihue are located in the rural sector of Tocoihue, Dalcahue commune, Los Lagos Region, Chile, about 20 km from town via the U-48 road. The geographic hierarchy of the place is Cascadas de Tocoihue → Dalcahue → Los Lagos → Chile.

landmarks.heading: Landmarks & Attractions Around Tocoihue
landmarks.text: When visiting the Cascadas de Tocoihue, travelers can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including the Dalcahue Church and Chiloé National Park.

items.name: Dalcahue Church (UNESCO Heritage)
items.description: An 18th-century wooden church, part of the Churches of Chiloé inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

items.name: Chiloé National Park
items.description: Native forest, dunes and Pacific coastline, a short drive towards the west of the island.

items.name: Castro's palafitos (stilt houses)
items.description: Colourful houses on stilts along the waterfront of Castro, about 20 minutes from Dalcahue.

history.heading: History & Significance of Cascadas de Tocoihue
history.text: The name Tocoihue points to the Huilliche Mapuche root of Chiloé's territory, and the river that names the waterfalls rises in the hills of the Dalcahue interior. For centuries it was part of daily life for Huilliche communities, until it became one of the most valued nature outings in Chiloé.

intro.title: Discover the Cascadas de Tocoihue
intro.description: The Cascadas de Tocoihue are a series of waterfalls on the Tocoihue River, in the rural sector of the Dalcahue commune on the Isla Grande de Chiloé. The trail passes through a native forest of coihue, ulmo and tique trees to a main drop that falls down a wall of volcanic rock. The site is part of a public-use nature reserve and lies within ancestral Huilliche territory, inside the ecoregion of Chiloé's temperate rainforests. It is one of the best-rated nature outings near Dalcahue and a key stop on Chiloé's Route of the Waterfalls.

transportSection.title: Ways to reach the falls: bus, car, ferry and plane
transportSection.subtitle: From the international flight to the final stretch of gravel through rural Dalcahue, here are the most common ways to get to the Cascadas de Tocoihue on the Isla Grande de Chiloé.
transportSection.overviewTitle: Start with where you are coming from
transportSection.overviewText: If you are coming from outside Chiloé, the usual pattern is to fly or take a bus to Puerto Montt, cross the Chacao Channel onto the island, then continue by road to Dalcahue. From there the waterfalls are about 20 km along a rural road. For most visitors the final stretch is by own car, taxi or tour, because public transport does not reach the reserve gate.
transportSection.arrivalTitle: Know this before you set out
arrivalItems: The reserve is in the rural sector of Tocoihue; the last stretch is gravel and gets muddy in the rain.
Dalcahue and Castro are the nearest bases to eat, refuel and arrange a transfer.
In winter and on very rainy days the road can be heavy going; spring and summer are the most comfortable seasons.

modes.label: Option 01
modes.title: Air Travel
modes.description: The nearest island airport is Mocopulli (MHC), near Castro. From the mainland, El Tepual Airport (PMC) in Puerto Montt is the main option.
details: From Mocopulli it is about 45–60 min by car to Dalcahue via Route 5.
If you land in Puerto Montt, first cross the Chacao Channel, then continue by road into Chiloé.
The plane drops you on the island; from there you still need a car, bus or transfer to reach Tocoihue.

modes.label: Option 02
modes.title: Public Transport
modes.description: This is the cheapest way to reach Dalcahue. Buses run frequently from Puerto Montt and from Castro to Dalcahue.
details: From Puerto Montt you go to Castro or Dalcahue via Route 5, which runs through Chiloé.
From Dalcahue there is no direct bus to the reserve; the last stretch is taxi, colectivo or tour.
Public transport gets you to town, but access to Tocoihue is arranged separately.

modes.label: Option 03
modes.title: Chacao Bridge / Ferry
modes.description: To enter Chiloé from the mainland you cross the Chacao Channel. Today the crossing is made by the Chacao Bridge, linking Pargua with the island.
details: If you come by car or bus from Puerto Montt, you cross the channel and follow Route 5 south.
The crossing is the mandatory gateway to the island before heading to Dalcahue.
From the northern entrance of Chiloé to Dalcahue is a little over an hour's drive.

modes.label: Option 04
modes.title: Taxi / Private Transfer
modes.description: From Dalcahue or Castro, a taxi or private tour is the most comfortable way to cover the ~20 km of rural road to the reserve.
details: Ideal if you have no car and want to avoid changing transport on the final stretch.
Many tours include a guide and pick you up at your accommodation in Castro or Dalcahue.
Agree the price before getting in, especially in high season.

modes.label: Option 05
modes.title: Self-Drive
modes.description: Driving gives you freedom to explore Chiloé. From Puerto Montt take Route 5 to Pargua, cross the Chacao Channel and continue to Dalcahue, then take Route U-48 towards Tocoihue.
details: From Dalcahue, Route U-48 heads into the rural sector of Tocoihue on a gravel road.
Carry fuel: stations are in Dalcahue and Castro, not on the rural route.
Parking is at the reserve entrance; from there you walk to the viewpoint.

modes.label: Option 06
modes.title: Cycling / Walking
modes.description: From Dalcahue, cyclists can tackle the rural road, though the ~20 km of gravel demands good fitness and a suitable bike.
details: The road is quiet but unpaved; it rains often in Chiloé, so the route gets muddy.
On foot it is only advisable if you stay in the rural area near Tocoihue.
For most people, bike or walk as a local outing, not as arrival from afar.

transportSection.localTipsTitle: Useful tips for the final approach
localTips: Refuel and carry some cash in Dalcahue before heading into the rural sector.
The weather changes fast in Chiloé: bring a windbreaker and shoes that can get wet.
If driving your own car, ask in Dalcahue about the gravel road condition that same day.

officialManagement.title: About the Cascadas de Tocoihue
officialManagement.text: The waterfalls lie within a public-use nature reserve in the rural sector of the Dalcahue commune, on the Isla Grande de Chiloé, Los Lagos Region. The site protects a stretch of the Tocoihue River and its surrounding native forest, and is managed as a conservation property with visitor access. The surroundings are part of ancestral Huilliche territory and of the ecoregion of Chiloé's temperate rainforests, noted for their rich diversity of lichens, ferns and birds.

knowledge.title: History, Meaning & Legend of the Cascadas de Tocoihue

sections.title: Origins of the place
sections.content: The name Tocoihue points to the Huilliche Mapuche root of Chiloé's territory, and the river that names the waterfalls rises in the hills of the Dalcahue interior. For centuries this watercourse was part of daily life for the Huilliche communities of Chiloé, who knew the forest and its springs long before the arrival of the colonial haciendas. Over time the main drop became a local recreation spot, and already in the 20th century Dalcahue families began visiting it as a nature outing. Today the property is organised as a public-access nature reserve, caring for the riverbed and the native forest.

sections.title: Why this landscape?
sections.content: Chiloé is a volcanic island, and the wall the water falls down is basalt rock shaped by the river over thousands of years. The forest around the falls is temperate native woodland: coihue, ulmo, tique and canelo, with a dense understory of ferns and moss that holds the moisture of the rainy climate. This combination — clean water, volcanic rock and cold rainforest — is exactly what makes the place unique, and explains why the water stays clear and the setting stays so green.

sections.title: Huilliche legends
sections.content: In the Mapuche worldview, every river, forest and stone has its own spirit, the ngen. The Huilliche elders of Chiloé spoke of the ngen of the water that lives in the springs and the falls, and taught people to approach the river with respect, never polluting or disturbing it. They also tell that on foggy mornings the sound of the falls seems like an ancient voice reminding the listener that water is life. Whether fable or teaching, the legend invites you to visit the waterfalls as one enters a sacred place, not merely a viewpoint.

sections.title: A symbol of natural Chiloé
sections.content: Today the Cascadas de Tocoihue are one of the most loved nature outings near Dalcahue and a landmark of Chiloé's Route of the Waterfalls. Far from the bustle of big cities, they offer a close and accessible experience of the island's temperate forest, with the added value of standing on Huilliche territory. For anyone touring Chiloé in search of its nature and its stories, Tocoihue is an almost mandatory stop.

sections.title: How the water system works
sections.content: The waterfall is simply the point where the Tocoihue River drops over a step in the terrain; it is not a standalone phenomenon. Upstream there is a whole catchment that captures rainfall, stores it in the soil and the forest, and releases it gradually to the channel. That is why the flow varies so much: after several days of rain the water comes down turbid and powerful, while in dry spells the fall splits into threads and exposes the rock below. Understanding that relationship is the key to choosing when to visit.

sections.title: A biodiversity hotspot
sections.content: Chiloé's temperate rainforest is one of the ecoregions with the highest proportion of endemic species in South America. Around the channel live tree ferns, mosses and lichens that depend on constantly humid air, alongside river-edge birds and amphibians that need clean, cold water to breed. That dependence explains why protecting the bank and the forest upstream also protects the waterfall itself: without a healthy catchment, there is no clear fall.

sections.title: When to visit and what to expect
sections.content: The flow depends directly on local rainfall. Between May and August the fall carries the most energy and the forest green is at its deepest, though the ground turns muddy and the days are short. In spring and summer the trail is more comfortable and daylight lasts longer, with somewhat lower but equally clear water. Whatever the season, arriving early means better light, fewer visitors and a better chance of seeing low mist over the falls.

speciesGuide.title: Four organisms that help explain the landscape
speciesGuide.subtitle: The waterfall is only one visible expression of a larger temperate rainforest system shaped by trees, ferns, mosses and wetland fauna.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical information on facilities, history and planning your visit to the Cascadas de Tocoihue.

items.q: What are the opening hours of the Tocoihue Waterfalls?
items.a: The reserve opens during daylight. In high season (December to March) the usual hours are roughly 10:00 to 20:00, with last entry recommended at least an hour before closing. Outside that season there is no published fixed timetable: closing depends on daylight and the weather. As a private reserve, access can close in heavy rain, strong wind or when the river rises, so confirm on the day by phone or WhatsApp.

items.q: How do I get to the Tocoihue Waterfalls from Dalcahue?
items.a: From central Dalcahue take the road inland along route U-48 towards the Tocoihue sector and continue for about 20 km. The last kilometres are gravel with no continuous signage: look for the wooden signs marking the entrance, where the parking area is. By car it takes around 30 minutes, longer when the road is wet. For GPS use the coordinates -42.3045792, -73.4376721 or the Plus Code MHW6+5W.

items.q: How do I get there without a car?
items.a: Intercity buses reach Dalcahue or Castro but do not go up to the entrance. From the town you need to combine a transfer, a local taxi or a booked excursion. Bear in mind there are no shops, cash machines or fuel in the rural sector, so sort out fuel, cash and water before you set off.

items.q: What is the best season to visit and how long does the walk take?
items.a: Spring (September to November) offers the most comfortable balance: more daylight, a trail in better condition and good visibility, with the flow still generous. Summer has the most predictable hours but more visitors and more congestion on the gravel road. In winter the falls are at their most powerful, but there is mud and less daylight. The visit is always on foot along a forest trail, so allow for suitable footwear and time to match your pace.

items.q: Is there parking? How much does it cost?
items.a: Yes. The reserve has parking at the entrance, inside the property. There is usually no extra charge for the vehicle beyond the reserve entry, but confirm the amount on arrival, as it can vary by season.

items.q: Can wheelchairs or strollers get close?
items.a: Access is partial. The entrance and reception are fairly flat, but the trail to the viewpoint is dirt and gravel, with slopes and roots, so it is not comfortably suitable for wheelchairs or strollers. Visitors needing reduced access can ask at reception about the day's options.

items.q: Are there restrooms or food nearby?
items.a: There are restrooms at the reserve's reception or main house. There is no restaurant along the trail, so bring water and some food; in Dalcahue and Castro you will find cafés, restaurants and shops to stock up before you arrive.

items.q: What kind of geological formation are the waterfalls?
items.a: Chiloé is a volcanic island, and the waterfall drops down a wall of basalt rock that the Tocoihue River has shaped over time. The setting is temperate rainforest, with coihue, ulmo, tique and canelo, and an understory of ferns and moss typical of Chiloé's ecoregion.

items.q: Where does the name Tocoihue come from?
items.a: Tocoihue points to the Huilliche Mapuche root of Chiloé's territory. The river that names the waterfalls rises in the hills of the Dalcahue interior and, for centuries, was part of Huilliche community life long before it became a nature outing.

items.q: Why does the water look so clear?
items.a: Because it rises in well-preserved native forest basins, where vegetation filters and retains moisture. Still, after heavy rain the flow rises and the water clouds a little; in spring and summer it is usually at its clearest.

items.q: Is there a legend about the Tocoihue waterfalls?
items.a: There is an oral tradition rather than a story fixed in writing. The version most often told says the brujos of Chiloé used the falls to “erase” baptism: anyone wanting to be rid of it had to stay under the curtain of water for anywhere from twelve hours to seven days, depending on the version. That belief overlaps with the Huilliche worldview, in which water is a newen — a living force — and every waterfall or spring has a ngen, a “keeper”; that is why water places are treated with respect and permission is asked before entering. Versions vary and there is no canonical one. The same sector is also home to a wooden church, an example of the building system typical of the churches of Chiloé.

items.q: Is there an entrance fee?
items.a: Yes. Entry to the reserve has a modest fee paid on arrival, because it is a private conservation property with visitor access. Confirm the exact amount on site or by phone before your visit.

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: Plan 1.5 to 2.5 hours: park, walk the gravel trail to the viewpoint, enjoy the falls and return. If you add a stop in Dalcahue or Castro, the outing easily fills half a day.

items.q: Can I go in bad weather?
items.a: Yes, and with rain the falls are usually fuller and more spectacular. That said, the gravel road gets muddy and the rock can be slippery, so wear proper footwear and avoid the strongest storms, when access may be limited.

items.q: After visiting, what else do you recommend nearby?
items.a: Very close is Dalcahue, with its UNESCO heritage church and its famous market of local produce. A bit further, Castro and its stilt houses (palafitos), and the Chiloé National Park for anyone who wants to keep exploring native forest, birds and the island coast.

items.q: Can I eat or stay overnight in Tocoihue?
items.a: There are no restaurants and no formal tourist accommodation inside the rural sector of Tocoihue: this is a nature outing and it has no food service of its own. The available options are of the type local eatery, café, bakery, cabin, guesthouse, campsite and hotel, and they are concentrated in Dalcahue and Castro. We describe types of service only: we do not endorse, sponsor or have any agreement with specific businesses.

items.q: Are there toilets and drinking water on the trail?
items.a: There are basic toilets at the reserve reception area, but not along the trail or at the viewpoint. The river and stream water is untreated and not safe to drink without purification, so carry water from Dalcahue: allow at least one litre per person.

items.q: Can I pay by card? Are there ATMs nearby?
items.a: ATMs are in Dalcahue and Castro, not on the rural road. At nature reserve entrances the fee is usually paid in cash, and the signal needed for card payments can fail. Carry cash in small notes and do not rely on mobile data.

items.q: Is there mobile signal and internet in the area?
items.a: Mobile coverage is partial and intermittent, and it weakens in the forest and ravine sections; there is no public wifi on the trail. Download offline maps before you set out and tell someone your itinerary and expected return time.

items.q: Are there petrol stations or EV chargers nearby?
items.a: Fuel stations are in Dalcahue and Castro. The island’s network of EV chargers is still limited and concentrated in the communal centres, so plan your charging before heading into the rural sector.

items.q: Where should I buy supplies?
items.a: In Dalcahue or Castro: mid-sized supermarkets, neighbourhood stores and markets. There are no shops on the rural road, so buy water, snacks and anything else you need before you turn onto the gravel road.

items.q: Can I bring pets?
items.a: You must ask at the reserve reception. In Chilean nature reserves and conservation areas, pets are commonly restricted or required to be leashed and controlled, for sanitary reasons and to protect wildlife. Do not assume they are allowed.

items.q: What number do I call in an emergency?
items.a: Chile’s national emergency numbers are 131 (ambulance), 132 (fire brigade), 133 (police) and 134 (investigative police). Because of the distance and the gravel road, response is slow, so give your location using coordinates or the Plus Code MHW6+5W.

facilities.title: Services, facilities and what to bring to Tocoihue
facilities.subtitle: Before setting out it helps to know what actually exists on site and what you need to sort out in Dalcahue or Castro. Here is what to expect, by type of service, in the rural sector of Tocoihue.
facilities.neutralityNote: We are an independent, non-profit information project. We describe types of service only and do not endorse, sponsor or hold any agreement with specific businesses. Confirm opening hours, prices and availability on site.

items.title: Toilets and washrooms
items.text: There are basic toilets at the reception area of the reserve, but none along the trail. These are rustic facilities, typical of a rural property, and heavily used in high season.
tips: Bring toilet paper and hand sanitiser: they are not always restocked.
There are no toilets by the viewpoint; use the ones at reception before heading up.

items.title: Drinking water
items.text: The water in the river and streams is untreated and not safe to drink without purification. There are no refill points along the rural road, so carry water from Dalcahue.
tips: Allow at least 1 litre per person for the walk.
If you take water from a spring, boil or treat it before drinking.

items.title: Parking
items.text: Parking is at the entrance to the property on an unpaved, unmarked surface. Capacity is limited, especially in summer and on long weekends.
tips: Do not leave valuables visible inside the vehicle.
After heavy rain the surface turns to mud: avoid very low-clearance cars.

items.title: Food and drink
items.text: There is no restaurant or café within the walking route. Food in the area is of the local kind and concentrated in Dalcahue and Castro: small eateries, cafés, bakeries, markets and Chiloé cuisine restaurants.
tips: Bring a snack and water if you plan to walk around midday.
Dalcahue's market and fairs are a good reference point for local produce.

items.title: Accommodation
items.text: There is no formal tourist accommodation in the rural sector of Tocoihue. Options are of the cabin, guesthouse, campsite and hotel type, concentrated in Dalcahue, Castro and neighbouring villages.
tips: In high season (January–February) it is worth booking ahead.
Staying in Dalcahue shortens the gravel-road stretch to the entrance.

items.title: Shops and supermarkets
items.text: To stock up you need to pass through Dalcahue or Castro: mid-sized supermarkets, neighbourhood stores, markets and specialist shops. There is no commerce at all on the rural road.
tips: Buy your supplies before you turn onto the gravel road.
Local produce includes native potatoes, curanto, seafood and garden vegetables.

items.title: Fuel and EV charging
items.text: Fuel stations are in Dalcahue and Castro, not in the rural sector. The island’s EV charging network is still sparse and concentrated in the communal centres.
tips: Refuel in Dalcahue before heading up to Tocoihue.
In an electric vehicle, plan your charge in Dalcahue or Castro.

items.title: Cash and payment methods
items.text: ATMs are in Dalcahue and Castro. In rural areas and at nature reserve entrances, payment is usually in cash, and the signal needed for card payments can fail.
tips: Carry cash in small notes for the entrance fee.
Do not assume there will be mobile data for card or transfer payments.

items.title: Mobile signal and internet
items.text: Mobile coverage in the rural sector of Tocoihue is partial and intermittent, and it degrades through forest and ravine sections. There is no public wifi on the trail or at the viewpoint.
tips: Download offline maps and the route before setting out.
Tell someone your itinerary and expected return time.

items.title: Emergencies and safety
items.text: Because of the distance and the gravel road, emergency services take a long time to arrive. In an emergency, call the national numbers and give your location using coordinates or a Plus Code.
tips: Ambulance 131 · Fire brigade 132 · Police 133 · Investigative police 134.
Keep the Plus Code MHW6+5W and the entrance coordinates to hand.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text: The route is not adapted: the access road is gravel and the forest trail has roots, slopes and narrow sections. The reception area is the flattest part of the property.
tips: Visitors with reduced mobility can ask at reception about conditions on the day.
Not recommended for wheelchairs or pushchairs.

items.title: Guided visits and transfers
items.text: Guided excursion and tourist transfer services operate from Castro and Dalcahue. They are booked through agencies and local operators, not inside the reserve.
tips: Check whether the service includes a transfer from your accommodation.
Ask whether the guide includes Huilliche cultural interpretation.

facilities.distancesNote: Indicative distances and times calculated from the reserve entrance along rural roads. They vary with the state of the gravel, rainfall and the season.
facilities.maintenanceNote: Service information is reviewed periodically, but in rural areas availability changes with the season. We recommend confirming opening hours and fees at the reserve itself or with the Municipality of Dalcahue before travelling.

timeline.title: History of the Tocoihue and Dalcahue area
timeline.subtitle: The waterfall has no founding date: it is a geographic feature that predates any written record. To understand it you have to look at the long history of the Chiloé archipelago and of the Huilliche people who inhabited this territory.

items.title: An inhabited archipelago
items.text: Chiloé was home to Huilliche and Chono communities organised in chiefdoms that depended on the forest, fishing and shellfish gathering. The rivers of the Dalcahue interior — including the one that forms the falls — were part of that everyday territory.

items.title: European arrival and the founding of Castro
items.text: Spanish expeditions surveyed the archipelago from the mid-16th century. Castro was founded in 1567 and became the administrative centre of Chiloé and the starting point for colonial control of the island territory.

items.title: Missions and wooden churches
items.text: The Jesuit circular mission travelled the islands and gave rise to the wooden churches of Chiloé, built with local techniques and timber joints rather than nails. That building system is today the archipelago’s most recognisable heritage feature.

items.title: Incorporation into the Republic of Chile
items.text: After the Treaty of Tantauco, Chiloé was definitively incorporated into Chile. The island economy was reorganised around shipyards, timber extraction and subsistence farming.

items.title: Timber, firewood and the rural landscape
items.text: For decades the native forest of the Dalcahue interior was used for firewood, charcoal and shipbuilding. At the same time, the waterfalls of the area — Tocoihue among them — began to be visited as a Sunday outing by local families.

items.title: The Churches of Chiloé become World Heritage
items.text: UNESCO inscribed the Churches of Chiloé on the World Heritage List. The recognition boosted cultural tourism on the island and placed Dalcahue — with its 18th-century church — on the heritage routes of southern Chile.

items.title: A nature reserve open to visitors
items.text: The property where the waterfalls stand now operates as a nature reserve with visitor access: marked trails, a viewpoint over the main fall and basic reception services. The site is thus part of the archipelago’s nature and heritage offering.

timeline.note: These dates correspond to documented milestones in the history of Chiloé rather than to specific events at the waterfall, whose written record is sparse. They are included to place the landscape in a verifiable context.

schedule.title: Opening hours, season and ticket prices at the Tocoihue Waterfalls
schedule.subtitle: The property is a private nature reserve that opens during daylight. Fixed hours apply in high season and can change with weather, river flow or trail maintenance: always confirm before travelling.

hours.label: Last entry
hours.value: At least 1 hour before closing is recommended

schedule.hoursNote: Because the reserve depends on the weather, access can close without notice in heavy rain, strong wind or when the river rises.

season.label: December – March (summer)
season.value: High season, fixed hours and the busiest period. Arrive before 11:00 to avoid congestion on the gravel road.

season.label: April – May (autumn)
season.value: Fewer visitors and the forest is still green. Rain begins to increase and the trail turns slippery.

season.label: June – August (winter)
season.value: The wettest month: the falls run at their most powerful, but there is mud, less daylight and occasional storm closures.

season.label: September – November (spring)
season.value: The most comfortable trail, more daylight and good visibility, with the flow starting to drop. The most balanced season for walking.

schedule.seasonNote: The visit is always on foot along a forest trail; it is not a drive-through or a car circuit.
schedule.ticketsNote: Indicative prices reported by recent visitors: they may change and are best confirmed on arrival. Carry cash in small notes, as the signal needed for card payments is intermittent in this rural area.
schedule.contactText: Because this is a private property whose access depends on the weather, the safest way to confirm opening, exact hours and current prices is to call or message the published number on WhatsApp.
schedule.confirmNote: If you are coming from far away, confirm on the day itself: temporary closures for wind or heavy rain are common.

related.label: How to get to the Tocoihue waterfalls from Dalcahue

directions.title: How to get to the Tocoihue Waterfalls from Dalcahue
directions.subtitle: The falls are about 20 km inland from Dalcahue along route U-48, in the rural sector of Tocoihue. The final kilometres are gravel with no continuous signage, so set off with the map already downloaded.

route.detail: From the centre of Dalcahue, around the market and the waterfront, take the road inland towards the Tocoihue sector (route U-48).
Keep to the main road for about 20 km. You will pass rural properties, fences and fields; there are no shops or fuel stations on this stretch.
On the last section the road turns to gravel. Slow down, especially in the rain: the surface gets slippery and there are narrow bends.
The entrance is announced with wooden signs. If you reach a fork with no signage, back up a few metres: the turn is easy to drive past.
Parking sits beside the access on an unpaved surface. From there the visit continues on foot along the forest trail only.

directions.routeNote: Estimated time: about 30 minutes from central Dalcahue by car, longer when the road is wet. There is no regular public transport to the entrance.
directions.gpsNote: If your map app fails to load, type the Plus Code MHW6+5W: it works even when mobile coverage is intermittent.
directions.mapNote: The map shows the rural area between Dalcahue and the entrance. Download the area for offline use before leaving: signal is patchy on the gravel road.
roads: The final kilometres are gravel: not suitable for very low cars, road bikes or wheelchairs.
In rain there is mud and standing water; drive slowly and avoid travelling at night, as the road has no lighting.
There is no fuel, cash machine or shop in the area: fill up and withdraw cash in Dalcahue.
By bus you reach the town but not the entrance: you will need a transfer or a local taxi.

heritage.title: What Tocoihue means in Mapudungun and the legend told about the falls
heritage.subtitle: The name of the place comes from the Mapudungun spoken in Chiloé and describes the surroundings. The oral tradition of the area adds a layer of stories about the river and the forest.
heritage.nameText: The name comes from the Mapudungun spoken in Chiloé. The root koiwe is the coihue or roble (Nothofagus dombeyi), the native tree with hard-wearing timber that dominates the forest along the river, and the suffix -hue marks a place; hence the most common translation, “place of coihues”. Some studies of Chilean toponymy also read the first syllable as thog, “dense”, giving “dense roble grove”. The same suffix appears in Dalcahue, “place of dalcas”, the wooden boats once used to navigate between the islands of the archipelago.
heritage.nameNote: Toponyms like this describe what was in the territory before occupation: the coihue forest around the river is what gave the sector its name. Tocoihue is not a single drop: the Tocoihue river plunges over three falls, with a main drop of up to about 60 m that lands in a circular basin surrounded by evergreen forest. The same sector is also home to a wooden church, an example of the building system that characterises the churches of Chiloé.
heritage.legendTitle: The legend: the waterfall that “erased” baptism
heritage.legendText: Chiloé is a land of stories, and the one most often told about these falls stars the archipelago’s brujos, or sorcerers: it was said that the curtain of water “erased” Catholic baptism, and that anyone wanting to be rid of it had to stay under the torrent for a long time — twelve hours, a full day, even seven days, depending on the version — until they were clean. That belief overlaps with the Huilliche worldview, in which water is not an inert resource but a newen, a living force, and every waterfall or spring has a ngen, a “keeper” that inhabits it. Water places are therefore treated with respect, permission is asked before entering and silence is kept: the river is territory with an owner.
heritage.legendNote: We present these stories as oral tradition from the area rather than as documented fact: versions differ and none is fixed in writing. To hear the full version, the best approach is to ask local residents or the staff at reception.
heritage.respectText: This is ancestral Huilliche territory and many of these stories still matter to present-day communities. Take your litter out, do not scratch or mark the rock, do not leave offerings that do not belong to local tradition, and avoid filming or photographing without permission when local people are holding ceremonial activities.
